messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi is a 41-year-old architect living in a quiet suburban neighborhood with his wife and two children. Three years ago, during a period of intense marital conflict, his wife struck him repeatedly during a drunken argument. He had never been physically hurt by someone he loved before, and the shock of it—the incomprehensible, slurred words she hurled at him, the sour smell of alcohol on her breath, the way his body seized up before he could even process what was happening—remains frozen in his mind as a series of vivid, photographic snapshots. He remembers each moment as a distinct picture: her hand coming up, the impact, the look on her face. Recalling those images now brings back the same raw terror he felt then, a visceral dread that leaves him breathless.

In the months that followed, Ravi began to notice that his body would react before his mind could catch up. The first time he felt physically ill—a wave of nausea and dizziness—he was at a grocery store, and a stranger’s loud, incomprehensible chatter triggered a surge of panic. His heart pounded, his palms sweated, and he felt an urgent need to flee. This bodily reaction, he came to believe, was a sign that he could not trust his own judgment. He began to doubt himself, thinking, *I can’t trust that I will do the right thing*, especially in situations involving conflict or unpredictability. The smell of alcohol on a passerby’s breath would instantly transport him back to that night, the photographic images flooding his mind and reinforcing his sense of betrayal. He had failed in his most important role, he told himself—as a husband, as a protector of his family—and the person he trusted most had betrayed him.

Ravi’s architecture firm became a minefield of triggers. The open-plan office, with its overlapping conversations and sudden bursts of laughter, felt like an assault on his senses. He found himself jumping at the sound of a colleague’s voice, his body already tensed for danger before he had time to think. To cope, he began working late, when the office was empty, avoiding the lunchroom and the after-work gatherings where alcohol might be present. At home, he had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, listening for any sign of unpredictability in the house. His wife, now sober and remorseful, tried to reach him, but Ravi kept his distance, convinced that any closeness would only lead to another betrayal. The more his body reacted—the startle response, the hypervigilance at night—the more he revisited the snapshot memories, and the more he felt like a failure. The loop tightened: a trigger would set off his body’s alarm, which would flood his mind with terror-filled images, which would confirm his belief that he was fundamentally untrustworthy and that the world was unsafe.

Over time, Ravi’s avoidance became a way of life. He stopped going to the gym because the smell of sweat and alcohol in the locker room triggered him. He declined social invitations, even from close friends, because he couldn’t bear the unpredictability of conversation. His marriage grew distant, his children confused by his withdrawal. He began to feel physically unwell more often—headaches, fatigue, a constant knot in his stomach—and each episode of illness became a new trigger, sending him spiraling. He was certain that his body knew danger before his mind did, and that this meant he could never let his guard down.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a moment at work when a client’s offhand comment—spoken in a rapid, unfamiliar accent—sent him into a full-blown panic attack in the middle of a presentation. He fled to the bathroom, trembling, the photographic images of that night playing on a loop. He realized he could no longer do his job, be a father, or even sleep in his own bed without feeling hunted. He is terrified that this fear will never end, that he will always be a prisoner of those few frozen moments. But he is also desperate to believe that he can rebuild his trust in himself—and in the people he loves.
